title: Matched parentheses
label: idb
statement:
Given a string containing alphanumeric characters and parentheses, determine whether the parentheses are correctly matched.

Examples:

()()()() → true

((45+)*a3) → true
provenance: Supplied by you from InterviewDB — the statement above is **verbatim**. Corroboration: InterviewDB + your own list + a 2025 report of this exact variant.
clarify: Only `(` and `)` are brackets; `[` and `{` are ordinary characters.
Every non-bracket character is ignorable, including `+` and `*`.
Null is valid rather than an exception.

1.q: Null? No parentheses? Long nested input?
1.a: Balanced; balanced; counter is O(1) so depth is free

2.a: One bracket type needs only a depth count — O(1) space

4.a: Stream characters; the counter never grows

flaw.ctx: You asked for a check that parentheses are matched.
flaw.answer: Equal counts are necessary, not sufficient: `")("` has one of each and returns **true**. The depth must never go negative at any prefix.
flaw.fix: One counter: +1 on `(`, −1 on `)`, return false the moment it goes below zero, true if it ends at zero.
flaw.verified: compiled against this problem's stage tests by npm run verify

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Given a string containing alphanumeric characters and parentheses, determine whether the parentheses are correctly matched.
> 
> Examples:
> 
> ()()()() → true
> 
> ((45+)*a3) → true

Scan a string and decide whether its round brackets nest correctly. Everything that is not a bracket is noise.

One boolean. Not the position of the error, not the depth — though both are natural follow-ups and nearly free.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
The first sentence says the string contains "alphanumeric characters and parentheses". The second example is `((45+)*a3)`, which contains `+` and `*` — **neither of which is alphanumeric**.

So either the description is loose and it means "parentheses plus other stuff", or the examples are illustrative of a wider input. The safe implementation treats **every** non-parenthesis character as irrelevant, which satisfies both readings. Say that you noticed and that you chose the permissive reading; the alternative — validating the character set and rejecting `+` — would fail the supplied example.

| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| Only `(` and `)` are brackets; `[` and `{` are ordinary characters. | If square and curly brackets must also match, the counter is **wrong** — `([)]` has balanced counts and is invalid. That needs the stack. This is the clarification worth asking. |
| Every non-bracket character is ignorable, including `+` and `*`. | Forced by the second supplied example. Validating the character set instead would reject it. |
| An empty string is valid. | Vacuously true. Cheap to state and the first thing a test checks. |
| Null is valid rather than an exception. | Debatable. Whichever you choose, say it — silently dereferencing null is the actual error. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
The reflex answer to any bracket question is "use a stack", and here the more useful observation is **why you do not need one**.

A stack exists to remember *what* was opened, so that a closing bracket can be matched against the right kind. With exactly one bracket type there is nothing to remember: every `(` is identical to every other `(`, so a `)` can only ever be matched against "the most recent open one", and all you need to know is **how many** are open. A single integer replaces the stack, and the space goes from O(n) to O(1).

Two conditions make it correct, and they are genuinely different. The counter must never go negative *during* the scan — that catches `)(`, which has a final count of zero and is invalid. And it must be exactly zero *at the end* — that catches `(()`. Checking only the final value accepts `)(`; checking only for negatives accepts `(()`. Both are needed, and being able to name the string each one catches is the whole of this question.

Then say where it stops working. The moment a second bracket type exists, counting fails, because `([)]` has balanced counts of both and is still wrong. Order now matters, and the stack is what records order. Knowing *which constraint* forces the stack is worth more than reaching for it by default.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** Repeatedly scan the string deleting every adjacent `()` pair, until a pass makes no change. Valid if the remaining string has no brackets. *O(n²) time — each pass is O(n) and there can be n/2 passes on a nested string — and O(n) space for the rewritten string.*

**Why not good enough.** It is correct, which is worth noting, and it is a reasonable first thing to say. It is quadratic on exactly the input you would use to test it, `((((()))))`. The single-pass version is not an optimisation of it so much as the observation that the repeated deletion is only ever tracking a depth, and the depth can be tracked directly.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | A string of mixed characters |
| TRANSFORMATION | Ignore everything that is not `(` or `)` |
| DATA STRUCTURE | One integer. For the multi-type case, a `Stack<char>`. |
| ALGORITHM | Increment on `(`, decrement on `)`; fail on a negative count; require zero at the end |
| OUTPUT | A boolean |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Null or empty → true.
- Walk the string. On `(`, increment.
- On `)`, decrement; if the count is now negative, return false **immediately**.
- Ignore every other character.
- At the end, return whether the count is exactly zero.

- **One bracket type only.** That is the constraint that changes the answer, and it is easy to miss because the problem looks like LeetCode 20.
- Two failure modes, and they are different: a `)` arriving with nothing open, and the string ending with something still open.
- Non-bracket characters never affect validity.
- A single pass, and with one bracket type, O(1) space.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| A single counter, not a stack | With one bracket type the identity of the open bracket carries no information, so only the count does. O(1) space instead of O(n), and the early-exit check is one comparison. |
| `Stack<char>`, only for the multi-type version | Once there are several types, order matters, and the stack is the structure that records order. Introducing it before that is over-engineering; knowing exactly when it becomes necessary is the point. |
| A `Dictionary<char, char>` of closer → opener in the multi-type version | Rather than a switch. It makes adding a bracket type a data change instead of a code change, which is the kind of thing the Staff Coding module explicitly says it scores under extensibility. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**Why the negative check is inside the loop.** Moving it after the loop would accept `)(`, whose final count is zero. The invariant is "the count is never negative at any prefix", and an invariant about every prefix has to be checked at every prefix. Returning early is not an optimisation here; it is the correctness condition.

**Why the final check is `== 0` and not `<= 0`.** The count cannot be negative at the end, because the loop would have returned. So `<= 0` would be equivalent and misleading — it suggests a case that cannot happen. `== 0` states the intent: everything opened was closed.

**The `else if`, and what falls through.** `if ( ... ) else if ( ... )` with no final `else`. Every other character does nothing, which is the permissive reading of "alphanumeric characters and parentheses" and the only reading that accepts the supplied example.

**Why `IsBalancedMultiType` is kept alongside it.** Not as the answer, but to make the boundary concrete. It differs in one respect that matters: a closing bracket is checked against the specific opener on top of the stack, so `([)]` fails. Having both in front of you is the fastest way to answer "what if there were three bracket types" — and the test suite asserts that the counter says **true** to `([)]` while the stack says false, so the difference is documented rather than described.

**`stack.Count == 0` at the end of the multi-type version.** Same second failure mode as the counter’s `== 0`. Both versions need two checks; the stack version just spells the first one as `stack.Count == 0 || stack.Pop() != want`.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `IsBalanced` | O(n) | O(1) | One pass, one integer |
| `IsBalancedMultiType` | O(n) | O(n) | The stack can hold every character on `((((` |

**The space difference is the whole point of the question.** O(1) versus O(n) is not a micro-optimisation here — it follows from a property of the input, and noticing that property is what is being tested. It also matters for the streaming follow-up: a counter can validate an arbitrarily long stream in constant memory, and a stack cannot.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Empty string | true. |
| Null | true as written. State the choice. |
| No brackets at all | true — the count never moves. |
| `(` | false — caught by the final check. |
| `)` | false — caught by the negative check on the first character. |
| `)(` | false. The case that requires the in-loop check. |
| `(()` | false. The case that requires the final check. |
| Deeply nested, 1,000,000 characters | Fine. The counter is O(1) space; the stack version would allocate a million entries but still not overflow, since it is iterative. |
| `([)]` | **true** under the single-type reading. The case to clarify before coding. |

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**Now there are three bracket types.**

A `Stack<char>`. Push openers. On a closer, fail if the stack is empty or if the top is not the matching opener. Succeed only if the stack is empty at the end. Keep the pairing in a dictionary so a fourth bracket type is a data change.

*Trade-off:* O(n) space instead of O(1), for the ability to enforce ordering. There is no way around it: any structure that validates nesting of multiple types must remember the sequence of unclosed openers, and in the worst case that is the whole input.

**The input is a stream and does not fit in memory. Can you still validate it?**

For one bracket type, yes, trivially: the counter is the entire state, so an arbitrarily long stream validates in O(1) memory and you can reject the moment it goes negative. For multiple types you need the stack of unclosed openers, which in the worst case is the full stream — so the honest answer is that single-type streams are O(1) and multi-type streams are not.

*Trade-off:* If bounded memory is a hard requirement with multiple types, you have to bound the nesting depth instead and reject beyond it. That is a real protocol design decision — it is why JSON parsers ship with a maximum depth — and saying so connects the toy question to something real.

**Return the index of the first unmatched bracket.**

For an unexpected closer the index is the current position. For an unclosed opener, the counter cannot tell you **where** it was — so this follow-up forces a stack even with one bracket type, holding indices rather than characters. Return the top of the stack at the end.

*Trade-off:* This is the cleanest example of a requirement forcing a structure. Nothing about validity needed the stack; wanting to *report* the location does. Worth saying explicitly — it shows the structure choice was driven by requirements rather than habit.

**What about the `*` wildcard version, where `*` can be an opener, a closer or empty?**

Track a **range** of possible open counts: `lo` and `hi`. A `(` increments both, a `)` decrements both, a `*` decrements `lo` and increments `hi`. Clamp `lo` at zero, fail if `hi` ever goes negative, and succeed if `lo` reaches zero at the end.

*Trade-off:* Still O(n) time and O(1) space, which is surprising and is why the problem is liked. The alternative is two-directional greedy or DP, both heavier. I would not volunteer this unless asked, but recognising it as the interval-of-counts trick rather than a new idea is the useful part.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *Null? No parentheses? Long nested input?* — Balanced; balanced; counter is O(1) so depth is free

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Why not a stack?* — One bracket type needs only a depth count — O(1) space
